query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains the mechanism expected to operate across the test regime, predicts performance relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, specifies relevant temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes a controlled falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an ultra‐thin silver nanoparticle (or nano‐coating) layer to a CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy surface will promote the in situ formation of a silver-enriched lubricating interfacial layer during sliding wear from room temperature up to 800 °C, thereby maintaining a low friction coefficient and wear rate relative to the uncoated alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy produced via laser 3D printing, with a relatively coarse-grained microstructure and no surface modification.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin silver nanoparticle or nano‐coating onto the alloy surface (or otherwise promote in situ diffusion of Ag) prior to sliding wear tests.
generation.conditions: Dry sliding in ambient air across a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, using sliding loads on the order of 10–100 mN and speeds typical of tribological studies.
generation.structural_mediator: The in situ formation of an Ag-rich, self-lubricating interfacial layer that remains present across the tested temperature range.
generation.mechanism: During sliding, frictional heating facilitates Ag diffusion and tribo-chemical interactions that cause the Ag particles to coalesce on the surface. This lubricating film lowers the surface shear strength and reduces direct metal-to-metal contact and plastic deformation, similar to reactive wear protection observed in Ag-containing alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the uncoated CoCrFeNi, the Ag-coated alloy is expected to exhibit a lower and more stable friction coefficient and reduced wear rate across the full temperature regime as the Ag film actively lubricates the interface, especially at elevated temperatures where diffusion is enhanced.
generation.baseline: Uncoated CoCrFeNi alloy, which in prior studies demonstrates higher friction and wear (in part due to unstable oxide film formation and plastic deformation) under similar sliding conditions.
generation.boundary: The expected benefits are anticipated only under dry sliding in ambient air, for temperatures between room temperature and 800 °C, and for applied loads and sliding speeds typical of the referenced sliding tests. Effects beyond these conditions are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Ag diffusion and film formation under variable thermal conditions, as well as the quantitative reduction in friction and wear, remain to be fully determined. Optimization of the coating thickness and adhesion may be required to ensure durability across the entire temperature range.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel pin-on-disk sliding wear tests comparing uncoated CoCrFeNi samples with samples that have received a thin Ag nanoparticle coating. Tests will be performed in ambient air over a temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C under identical loads and sliding speeds.
measurements: Wear volume loss (quantified via interferometric surface scans)
Surface morphology and composition (using SEM and XPS/EDS to detect the presence and continuity of the Ag-rich film)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If, under the specified testing conditions, the Ag-coated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant decrease in friction coefficients and wear rates compared to the uncoated CoCrFeNi—or if the Ag film does not remain intact and active throughout the full temperature range—the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Wear-related energy and material loss cost over 2500 Billion Euro per year. Traditional wisdom suggests that high-strength materials reveal low wear rates, yet, their plastic deformation mechanisms also influence their wear performance. High strength and homogeneous deformation behavior, which allow accommodating plastic strain without cracking or localized brittle fracture, are crucial for developing wear-resistant metals. Here, we present an approach to achieve superior wear resistance via in-situ formation of a strong and deformable oxide nanocomposite surface during wear, by reaction of the metal surface with its oxidative environment, a principle that we refer to as ‘reactive wear protection’. We design a TiNbZr-Ag alloy that forms an amorphous-crystalline oxidic nanocomposite surface layer upon dry sliding. The strong (2.4 GPa yield strength) and deformable (homogeneous deformation to 20% strain) nanocomposite surface reduces the wear rate of the TiNbZr-Ag alloy by an order of magnitude. Here, we propose an alloy design concept based on an enthalpy-guided approach to promote formation of solid solution nanocrystals, rather than crystalline oxide nanoparticles, in the amorphous matrix during wear. This structure enables a high strength and homogeneous plastic deformation of the friction-induced oxidic nanocomposite surface layer. We realize this concept in a multi-component (TiNbZr)75Ag25 (at.%) alloy, by blending a TiNbZr medium-entropy alloy with Ag to create the desired self-lubricating nanostructure upon wear exposure. A ball-on-disk sliding test at a maximum contact stress of 1.0 GPa reveals that the (TiNbZr)75Ag25 alloy exhibits a friction coefficient of around 0.09 in air. The tribological contact introduces environmental O into the alloy, facilitating new atomic coordination with large negative enthalpy of mixing, which enhances the alloy’s glass-forming ability. Besides, Ag has a positive enthalpy of mixing with Nb (+16 kJ/mol), which serves as a thermodynamic driving force for the nucleation of Ag nanocrystals from the amorphous matrix.
